Dear Chetan,
You asked how I'm holding up while the scholarship list is still not out. Honestly, the first week I refreshed the portal every hour and barely slept. Then Mausi made me write two columns on the back of an old calendar.
Left side: things I can move. I finished the fee-waiver form, emailed the hostel warden about a cheaper room, and fixed two tuition students for Saturday mornings. Right side: the committee's decision, the date, the number of seats. That column I read once a day and then leave alone.
It still itches, not knowing. But yesterday I went a whole evening without checking, and it felt like a muscle getting a little stronger.
Come over Sunday? I'll make chai.
Lokesh

So, Dilnaz, you know my little brother Sonu took the overnight train to Pune alone last month? I was a mess. I wanted to track every station, call him every hour, make him send photos of his berth.
Then around ten at night I caught myself and asked, okay, what can I actually do from here? I could make sure he had the charger, the uncle's number at the other end, and snacks. Done, all packed.
The train running late, who sits in his compartment, whether he sleeps, none of that was mine to hold. So I told him, one message when you board, one when you wake. Then I put my phone face-down and watched a film with Amma, who kept saying, 'See, Chandrika, the world hasn't ended.'

At the temple fair in Kodur, Pranav lost the slow-cycle race to Ganga for the second year. That evening he wheeled his cycle to the dry canal bank and practised balancing, feet up, counting under his breath. 'If I practise every day, next year I'll win,' he told his grandmother.

passage:
My little sister Gargi came home on Tuesday and didn't touch her paratha. That never happens. She kept picking at the tablecloth.
Later I heard her ask Mummy, very quietly, 'If your best friend copies in a test and you saw, are you a bad friend if you tell?'
She didn't say who, but Simran is her best friend, so I guessed.
Mummy didn't scold or give a lecture. She pulled Gargi onto her lap, though Gargi is nearly too big for that. 'Both answers have something good in them,' she said. 'What are you most scared of?'
Gargi whispered something I couldn't hear. They talked till the pressure cooker whistled twice.
I don't know what Gargi decided. But she ate dinner, and she hugged Mummy extra long before bed.

qa.a: Her paratha.

qa.q: What does Gargi picking at the tablecloth suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she was troubled and torn, worried that telling on her best friend would make her a bad friend.

qa.q: What choice did Mummy make when Gargi asked her question, and why did it help?
qa.a: Mummy chose not to scold or lecture and asked what Gargi feared most, which let Gargi think it through without shame.

qa.q: How might Simran be affected by whatever Gargi decides?
qa.a: Simran might face a hard talk or the teacher finding out, but could also learn that a caring friend noticed, depending on Gargi's choice.

grounding: Shows, through a sibling's eyes, a child torn between honesty and loyalty to a best friend, and a parent who helps her think rather than shaming her.
